5.text: I am not aware of the occurrence of any soapstone kettles or lamps on

6.text: the Asiatic side,¹ but the customs of the Chukchee concerning the taking

7.text: from the cliffs of pieces of sandstone fit for the manufacture of lamps cor-

8.text: respond to those of the American Eskimo regarding soapstone. Thus every

9.text: piece of sandstone has to be “bought” from the cliff with a little blubber or

10.text: with a small piece of tobacco-leaf. The man going for sandstone has to

11.text: strip to the waist, or in winter at least to take off his outer coat, or else the

12.text: displeasure of the “owner of the place”² will bring on a heavy storm.

13.text: The clay kettle of northeastern Asia, as well as the soapstone kettle of

14.text: arctic America, is evidently one of the contrivances of the Maritime people.

15.text: Its elongated rectangular form is adapted to the shape of the lamp over

16.text: which it was hung in cooking. Perhaps in former times a square frame of

17.text: poles connected by cross-bars was used to suspend it, as is the case with the

18.text: American Eskimo. The Chukchee woman, when cooking out of doors, often

19.text: builds, instead of the wooden tripod generally used in Siberia, a square frame

20.text: of sticks with cross-pieces at the top. Nowadays, however, the clumsy clay

21.text: vessels have long been superseded by copper and iron kettles and teapots.

22.text: No special frame is used for them in the sleeping-room, and the kettles are

23.text: suspended simply on a peg or a hook fastened to the wooden frame of the wall.

24.text: I have already spoken about the hooks used for hanging the kettle in

25.text: the outer tent. The Reindeer Chukchee of the Omolon employ for this purpose

26.text: a special pole, which is fastened in an upright position near the hearth, with

27.text: the upper end protruding through the vent-hole. The pole is made from the

28.text: slender trunk of a larch-tree, and one of the branches is retained. The line

29.text: of the kettle-hook is tied to it. The pole is called “single Jack,” “single man”

30.text: (yanřaᵋ-laˊul), and is used also in some of the Koryak camps.

31.text: BONE-BREAKING SET. — Another important household utensil, especially

32.text: with the Reindeer Chukchee, is the bone-breaking set (Fig. 105), which con-

33.text: sists of several stone mauls (Fig. 105, b), a large flat stone upon which to

34.text: lay the bones, and a flat cylindrical vessel made out of walrus-hide, and serving

35.text: as a receptacle for the broken bones (Fig. 105, a).
